summary: At a Pharisee’s dinner, a sinful woman weeps over Jesus’ feet and anoints them; Jesus tells a story of two debtors and declares her sins forgiven.
key_insight: Jesus’ story makes love the fruit of forgiveness, not its price: the debtor forgiven more loves more. So His last word to the woman is about her faith, not her love: “Your faith has saved you.”
story: One of the Pharisees, a man named Simon, invited Jesus to eat with him. Jesus went to his house and took His place at the table.

A woman of that city, known as a sinner, learned that Jesus was dining there. She came with an alabaster flask of fragrant oil and stood behind Him at His feet, weeping. She began to wash His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair. She kissed His feet again and again and anointed them with the oil.
Simon watched and said to himself, “This Man, if He were a prophet, would know who and what manner of woman this is who is touching Him, for she is a sinner.”

Jesus answered the thought Simon had not spoken: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” “Teacher, say it.” A creditor had two debtors, Jesus said. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Neither could pay, so he freely forgave them both. “Tell Me, therefore, which of them will love him more?” Simon answered, “I suppose the one whom he forgave more.” “You have rightly judged,” Jesus said.

Then He turned toward the woman and said to Simon, “Do you see this woman?” Simon had given Him no water for His feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for His head. She had washed His feet with her tears, had not stopped kissing them since He came in, and had anointed them with fragrant oil. “Therefore I say to you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom little is forgiven, the same loves little.”
To her He said, “Your sins are forgiven.” The other guests began to say among themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” But Jesus said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

fit.question: All four Gospels tell of a woman anointing Jesus, and in three of them the host is named Simon. Is Luke’s story the same event as the anointing at Bethany (Matthew 26, Mark 14, John 12)?

points.label: Two different scenes
points.text: Luke’s anointing happens in Galilee, early in Jesus’ ministry, in the home of a Pharisee. The Bethany anointing happens near Jerusalem days before His death, in the home of Simon the leper, with Lazarus at the table (Mark 14:3; John 12:2).

points.label: Different women, different complaints
points.text: Here an unnamed sinful woman weeps and is forgiven, and the objection is about her character. At Bethany, Mary the sister of Martha anoints Him (John 12:3), the objection is about wasted money, and Jesus speaks of His burial.

points.label: A common name
points.text: Simon was one of the most common Jewish names; the New Testament alone mentions nine different men called Simon. A shared name and an alabaster flask do not make one event.

fit.note: Two women honored Jesus in a similar way at two different times; the Gospels describe two events, not one event confused.
fit.short: Different times, places, hosts, women and complaints. Luke tells of an earlier anointing in Galilee, not Mary’s anointing at Bethany.

scene.label: Reclining at table
scene.text: At a formal dinner, guests lay on low couches around the table, leaning on one elbow with their feet stretched out behind them. That is how a woman could stand “at His feet behind Him.”

scene.label: An open house
scene.text: At such meals the doors often stood open, and people from the town could come in and watch from the edges of the room. The woman’s presence was not unheard of; what she did was.

scene.label: Missing courtesies
scene.text: A good host offered a guest water for dusty feet (Genesis 18:4), greeted him with a kiss, and might anoint his head with oil (Psalm 23:5). Simon offered none of these, and Jesus noticed.

scene.label: Two debts
scene.text: A denarius was a day’s wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). One debt was more than a year and a half of wages, the other less than two months. Both men had “nothing with which to repay.”

scene.label: Who was she?
scene.text: Luke does not name her. She is not Mary of Bethany. Scripture never says she was Mary Magdalene, who is introduced a few verses later as someone new (Luke 8:2). That idea was popularized centuries later, by Pope Gregory the Great around AD 591, and has no support in the text.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells this story. He places it right after the charge that Jesus was “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (7:34), so the reader sees what that friendship looks like at a real table. Luke often sets a respected man beside a despised outsider and shows which one truly receives Jesus.

seeing.reveals: Jesus knows exactly who the woman is and lets her touch Him anyway. He reads Simon’s unspoken thoughts, and He speaks a word only God can speak: “Your sins are forgiven.”
seeing.living: Simon thought he owed little, so he loved little. Love for Jesus does not grow by trying harder to love; it grows by seeing how much He has forgiven. Come to Him openly, without hiding, and hear Him say, “Go in peace.”
seeing.ponder: Are you more like Simon or the woman at Jesus’ feet, and what would change if you saw how large your debt was and how freely He cancelled it?

preaching.big_idea: Those who know they are forgiven much love Jesus much.
outline: A sinner at the Savior’s feet (36–38)
A host who judged in silence (39)
A verdict of forgiveness and peace (44–50)
preaching.watch_for: Simon decides Jesus cannot be a prophet because He does not know what kind of woman she is (v. 39). Jesus answers by reading Simon’s own heart, then asks, “Do you see this woman?” (v. 44). Simon saw a reputation; Jesus saw a forgiven person.
